s.g: A masculine patronymic suffix added to a given name ending in a hard (unpalatalized) consonant: son of

ety.text: Initialism of автомати́ческая коро́бка переключе́ния переда́ч (avtomatíčeskaja koróbka pereključénija peredáč).
Borrowed from French barrière f. Omitting several steps, from Vulgar Latin *barra.

s.g: bottle collector (an impoverished person who collects discarded bottles and sells them to recycling facilities)

ety.text: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic власъ (vlasŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vȏlsъ. Doublet of во́лос (vólos), the inherited East Slavic form.

s.g: to express oneself, to express one's opinion
to jump, hop, or leap while shouting excitedly
to accost, to rob, to mug

ety.text: Unclear. Attested by Dal in an 1842 manuscript on the Saint Petersburg criminal argot. Folk etymology connects the term to the acronym for Городско́е о́бщество призо́ра (Gorodskóje óbščestvo prizóra), the name of a former Saint Petersburg orphanage and workhouse for street children.

s.g: a kind of Priestless Old Believer (in particular, the one who prays through a special hole in the wall)
x: — Ты, ви́дно, не́христ, ды́рник. Дыре́ мо́лишься, — сказа́л ямщи́к, засо́вывая кнутови́ще за по́яс и оправля́я шлею́ на пристяжно́й.

s.g: to crush, to rumple, to crumple

ety.text: From мёд (mjod, “honey”) + -ед (-ed, “eater”). Compare медве́дь (medvédʹ, “bear”), composed of the same elements but going back to Proto-Slavic; and compare with Ukrainian медоїд (medojid).

x: Сано́вник э́тот, по ме́ткому замеча́нию одного́ его́ совреме́нника, «име́л си́льный ум и надме́нную фигу́ру», и така́я кра́ткая характери́стика верна́ и вполне́ доста́точна для представле́ния, како́е ну́жно име́ть о нём на́шему чита́телю.

ety.text: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic надъменъ (nadŭmenŭ, “inflated, blown up”), from Proto-Slavic *nadъmenъ (“inflated, blown up”) - passive past participle of *nadǫti (“inflate, blow up”). Doublet of наду́тый (nadútyj) and до́мна (dómna).

s.g: to fill out, to belly out, to swell out, to blow up, to inflate
plain, homely, not (very) attractive, not much to look at

ety.text: не- (ne-) + кази́стый (kazístyj) (which is now mainly used as: не очень казистый, не больно казистый, etc.). By surface analysis, не- (ne-) + каз(а́ться) (kaz(átʹsja)) + -и́стый (-ístyj).

s.g: to turn out, to be found, to prove (to be)
ellipsis of операти́вная па́мять (operatívnaja pámjatʹ); RAM

cartridge, shell, or round, consisting of the assembled bullet, casing, propellant, and primer

ety.text: Borrowed from German Patrone. Omitting several steps, from Latin patrōnus, from Latin pater.
Borrowed from French patron. Further from Latin patrōnus (the same as above).

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orkyta, which Pokorny connects to Ancient Greek ἄρκευθος (árkeuthos, “juniper”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷ- (“bend”). Also compare Latvian ērkšķis (“thorn bush”).
